strengths: Tackles a well-recognized and important open problem in predictive coding/equilibrium propagation research: the inability to train PC networks deeper than ~5-7 layers, which is a major obstacle to broader adoption of biologically-inspired/energy-based learning.

Provides a clear diagnostic experiment (layer-wise energy tracking, Figure 2 and appendix Figures 5-6) comparing PC to BP that visually demonstrates the energy imbalance phenomenon, giving a plausible causal narrative for the degradation.

Proposes a reasonably diverse set of complementary interventions (spiking precision, decaying precision, forward weight updates, BatchNorm freezing) each targeting different aspects of the identified problem, and shows they can be combined synergistically.

Extensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet) and four depths (VGG5/7/10/15), with 5 seeds, hyperparameter search details, and thorough ablation studies isolating each component's contribution.

Achieves results that substantially close the gap with backprop on 10- and 15-layer convolutional networks, a genuinely useful empirical advance in the field (Tiny ImageNet, 15 layers) previously only reached via hybrid BP/EP training.
Good reproducibility documentation: detailed appendix with architecture specs, hyperparameter search ranges, data augmentation and normalization details, and reported training-time comparisons.
Honest limitations section acknowledging that the theoretical understanding of the energy imbalance phenomenon and the biological implausibility introduced by forward updates remain open issues.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is only partially substantiated: Figure 2 shows that even with the proposed methods, the energy imbalance remains many orders of magnitude (e.g., still ~10^-10 vs ~10^-2 for BP), yet accuracy improves substantially — the paper does not rigorously establish why partial mitigation suffices, weakening the mechanistic story to more of a correlational conjecture.

Individual components behave inconsistently across settings: e.g., in Table 2 (Tiny ImageNet), Spiking Precision alone underperforms plain PC (18.36 vs 22.95 top-1), and Decaying+Forward Update is worse than Forward Update alone (21.95 vs 31.61); these inconsistencies are not analyzed in depth and undercut confidence in the proposed mechanisms as generally reliable rather than dataset/architecture-specific tricks.

The forward-update mechanism, which contributes most to the gains, is explicitly acknowledged to reduce biological plausibility (requiring storage of initial forward predictions), which is in tension with the paper's initial motivation (neuromorphic/analog hardware and local learning) — the significance of the contribution for the stated application domain is thus weakened.

On the hardest benchmark (Tiny ImageNet, VGG15), the best proposed combination (S+F) still slightly underperforms BP (42.51 vs 44.52 top-1 without BF; 53.04 vs 53.21 with BF), so the claim of 'comparable to backprop' is only approximately true and the paper's D+F variant is notably worse.

No empirical comparison to other recent approaches addressing depth in PC/EP models (e.g., hybrid BP/EP models, or the contemporaneous μPC method cited only in the conclusion), making it hard to judge how this method compares to alternative state-of-the-art solutions to the same problem.

The precision-weighting schemes (spiking, decaying) are heuristic constructions without theoretical grounding for why these particular functional forms should rebalance energy correctly; no principled derivation or convergence guarantee is provided.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'BarchNorm' typo, dense notation, some figures with small unlabeled text) slightly reduce clarity, and the energy-imbalance-vanishing-gradient analogy is asserted rather than formally connected.
